## Overview

- **Most common GI disease** requiring acute hospitalization
- **Incidence is rising**
- **~80%** have mild disease (symptoms resolve within 1 week)
- **~20%** develop **severe acute pancreatitis** with organ failure and/or necrotizing pancreatitis

::: {.callout-warning}
## Key Definition
**Necrotizing pancreatitis** = pancreatic parenchymal necrosis and/or peripancreatic fat necrosis
:::

## Clinical Significance

- Risk for **persistent SIRS** and/or **(multiple) organ failure**
- **30-60%** develop **secondary infection of necrosis** (most often 3-4 weeks after onset)
- When secondary infection occurs → **morbidity and mortality increase dramatically**
- **Overall mortality in severe pancreatitis: 15-30%** (vs. mild pancreatitis)


## Causes of Acute Pancreatitis

| Cause | Frequency |
|-------|-----------|
| **Gallstones** | 50-60% |
| **Alcohol** | 20% |
| Hypercalcemia | Less frequent |
| Hypertriglyceridemia | Less frequent |
| Medications | Less frequent |
| Hereditary causes | Less frequent |
| Sphincter of Oddi dysfunction | Less frequent |
| Pancreas divisum | Less frequent |
| Infections | Less frequent |

## Important Considerations

::: {.callout-important}
## Before Diagnosing "Idiopathic"
Must rule out causes with **therapeutic implications**:

- **Biliary sludge and gallstones** → seek by transabdominal or endoscopic ultrasonography
- **Pancreatic neoplasms** → consider in older patients with first episode and no clear etiology
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Diagnostic Challenge
CECT features may be obscured by inflammatory changes in neoplastic cases
:::


## Diagnostic Criteria (2 of 3 Required)

1. **Abdominal pain** consistent with acute pancreatitis
   - Acute onset
   - Persistent, severe, epigastric pain
   - Often radiating to the back

2. **Serum lipase or amylase** ≥ 3x upper limit of normal

3. **Characteristic findings** on CECT (less commonly MRI or transabdominal US)

## Imaging Considerations

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Usually
- First two criteria present
- **CECT NOT required** for diagnosis
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### CECT Helpful When
- Abdominal pain for several days
- Already normalized amylase and lipase levels
:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Caution with Early CECT
CECT in first **72-96 hours** often **fails to demonstrate** pancreatic necrosis and peripancreatic collections
:::


## 2012 Revised Atlanta Classification

### Three Categories Based on Complications

| Complications | Mild | Moderate | Severe |
|--------------|------|----------|--------|
| **Local** | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Transient organ failure** | No | Yes | Yes |
| **Persistent organ failure** | No | No | Yes |
| **Exacerbation of preexisting comorbidity** | No | Yes | Yes |

## Morphologic Classification

Based on local complications on diagnostic imaging:

- **Interstitial edematous pancreatitis**
- **Necrotizing pancreatitis**

## Local Complications - Collections (Table 93.2)

| Collection | Timing | Characteristics |
|-----------|--------|----------------|
| **Acute fluid collection** | < 4 weeks (edematous pancreatitis) | Homogeneous fluid density, confined by normal peripancreatic fascial planes, no definable wall |
| **Pseudocyst** | Usually > 4 weeks (edematous pancreatitis) | Adjacent to pancreas, well-circumscribed, homogeneous fluid density, well-defined wall, completely encapsulated |
| **Acute necrotic collection** | < 4 weeks (necrotizing pancreatitis) | Heterogeneous and non-liquid density, no definable wall, intrapancreatic and/or extrapancreatic |
| **Walled-off necrosis** | Usually > 4 weeks (necrotizing pancreatitis) | Heterogeneous and non-liquid density, well-defined wall, completely encapsulated, intrapancreatic and/or extrapancreatic |

## Practical Classification Issues

::: {.callout-note}
## Determinate Classification
Incorporates persistent organ failure and infected necrosis into a **"critical"** category
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Practical Issue
- **4-week period** for encapsulation is assumed but may differ among patients
- **Best practice**: Use actual presence of encapsulation (not time) to differentiate acute necrotic collection vs. walled-off necrosis
- **MRI** particularly helpful for fluid vs. solid debris
- **MRI** can be impractical in critically ill patients
:::


## Clinical Course Variability

- Unpredictable course
- Range: **full recovery in days** → **multiorgan failure and death within hours**

## Scoring Systems (Table 93.3)

| Score | Cutoff for Predicted Severe AP |
|-------|------------------------------|
| **APACHE II** | ≥ 8 in first 24h |
| **BISAP** | ≥ 3 in first 24h |
| **Modified Glasgow (or Imrie)** | ≥ 3 in first 48h |
| **Ranson** | ≥ 3 in first 48h |
| **Urea at admission** | > 60 mmol/L |
| **C-reactive protein** | > 150 U/L in first 72h |

## Limitations of Scoring Systems

::: {.callout-warning}
- No system with both **high negative predictive value** AND **high positive predictive value**
- Most popular scores have strengths and limitations
- **Persistent organ failure** is the **key determinant** for morbidity and mortality
:::

## Key Predictors

::: {.callout-important}
## IAP/APA Guidelines Recommendation
Use **persistent SIRS (> 48 hours)** as marker to predict severity
:::

- **(Early) multiorgan failure** associated with high mortality
- Persistent organ failure = key determinant in Revised Atlanta Classification

## Morphologic Scoring Systems

- Balthazar grade
- Pancreatic size index
- Extrapancreatic inflammation on CT score
- CT severity index
- Modified CT severity index

::: {.callout-note}
## CT vs. Clinical Scores
Study comparing all radiologic scoring systems showed **no advantage** of early CT on admission vs. more easily obtainable clinical scoring systems for predicting clinically severe AP and mortality
:::


## Traditional Biphasic Course

Two peaks of mortality: **early** and **late**

## Early Phase

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Characteristics
- Characterized by **SIRS**
- Lasts about **1-2 weeks**
- Cytokine cascades activated
- Host systemic response to local pancreatic disease
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Organ Failure
- May be present at first presentation
- Usually diagnosed at median **2 days** after admission
- **~50%** of early deaths have **NO infected necrosis** but suffer from **multiorgan failure**
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Modified Marshall Scoring System
Useful for assessing organ dysfunction
:::

## Late Phase

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Characteristics
- **CARS** (compensatory anti-inflammatory response syndrome)
- Can run protracted course: **weeks to months**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Organ Failure
- Related to **local complications**
- **Secondary infection** (e.g., infected pancreas necrosis)
- Occasionally pulmonary or urinary tract infection
:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Diagnostic Challenge in Late Phase
Difficult to determine cause of CARS reaction (infected necrosis vs. infection from another organ system)
:::

## Mortality Data

| Patient Group | Mortality |
|--------------|-----------|
| Organ failure in AP | **32%** |
| Both organ failure AND infected necrosis | **43%** |


## Early Supportive Measures

### Pain Management

- Intense abdominal pain = **presenting symptom** in vast majority
- Remains dominant feature during first days
- **No specific pain treatment regimen** for AP
- Use **WHO analgesic ladder**
- Exact place of pain management and physiologic/immunologic response still unknown

### Fluid Therapy

::: {.callout-important}
## WATERFALL Trial (2022)
- Randomized: goal-directed aggressive vs. moderate fluid resuscitation with lactated Ringer's
- **Stopped at interim analysis**
- Aggressive resuscitation → higher volume overload with **NO change in clinical outcome**
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Rationale for Fluids
- Correct/prevent intravascular hypovolemia
- Maintain microcirculation of pancreas
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Caution
- Uncontrolled aggressive fluid therapy → **morbidity and mortality**
- Monitor: heart rate, MAP, urinary output (0.5-1 mL/kg/h)
:::
:::

### Fluid Recommendations

| Parameter | Recommendation |
|-----------|---------------|
| **Fluid type** | Balanced physiologic solutions (Ringer lactate preferred) |
| **Avoid** | Normal saline (produces acidosis) |
| **Infusion rate** | 5-10 mL/kg/h |
| **Endpoint** | Resuscitation goals by vital parameters and urine production |

## Prevention of Infection

### Probiotics

::: {.callout-warning}
## PROPATRIA Trial
- Probiotics vs. placebo in predicted severe pancreatitis
- **NO effect** in reducing infectious complications
- **Unexpected higher rate** of bowel ischemia (9 vs. 0) and mortality (16% vs. 6%)
- **NOT recommended**
:::

### Antibiotics

::: {.callout-important}
## Key Finding
Most recent systematic reviews: **prophylactic IV antibiotics do NOT prevent infection** of (peri)pancreatic necrosis

**Antibiotics only indicated as THERAPY** (not prophylaxis) for:
- Proven infection
- Strong clinical suspicion of infected necrosis
:::

### Selective Decontamination

- Reduces mortality in general ICU patients
- Tested in AP: beneficial effects on **morbidity** but **NO impact on mortality**
- Use should be weighed against potential for:
  - Increased antibiotic resistance
  - Fungal colonization

## Nutrition

::: {.callout-important}
## PYTHON Trial
- Early nasoenteric tube feeding within 24h vs. oral diet with tube feeding only if not tolerated after 72h
- **Routine early nasoenteral nutrition did NOT reduce** composite endpoint of infection or mortality
- **69%** in on-demand group tolerated oral diet without tube feeding
:::

### Recommendations

- **Enteral nutrition** superior to parenteral in predicted severe AP
  - Reduces organ failure, infected necrosis, mortality
  - Mechanism: reduced gut permeability, less bacterial overgrowth/translocation

- **Enteral nutrition recommended only when oral diet not tolerated** during first 3-5 days

- **Practical approach**: Many patients tolerate some oral nutrition but not enough for caloric/protein demands
  - May receive some enteral + remainder parenterally

- **Endoscopically placed gastrojejunostomy feeding tubes**
  - Effective in early and mid-disease phases
  - Permit gastric decompression (many have gastric ileus)
  - Deliver nutrition beyond ligament of Treitz


## Role of ERCP and Papillotomy: Indications

::: {.callout-important}
## Urgent ERCP with Sphincterotomy
**ONLY indicated for:**
- **Biliary pancreatitis with concurrent cholangitis**
:::

## Evidence

| Scenario | Recommendation |
|----------|---------------|
| Mild biliary AP + no symptomatic CBD stones/cholangitis | **No evidence** ERCP beneficially influences course |
| Predicted severe AP without cholangitis | Evidence **conflicting** |

## APEC Trial

- Dutch Pancreatitis Study Group randomized multicenter trial
- Early ERCP with sphincterotomy in predicted severe AP without cholangitis
- Bile duct stones or sludge found in **58%** of 83 patients undergoing urgent EUS on first hospital day
- All underwent immediate ERCP
- **No difference** in primary composite endpoint vs. historical controls

::: {.callout-note}
## Conclusion
In acute pancreatitis, **early ERCP is indicated in the setting of cholangitis**
:::


## Mild Biliary Pancreatitis

::: {.callout-important}
## PONCHO Trial
- Early cholecystectomy (just before discharge, after recovery, severe disease excluded) vs. interval cholecystectomy
- Early cholecystectomy **effectively reduces** recurrent gallstone-related complications
- **Very low added risk** of complications

**Recommendation: Early cholecystectomy after mild biliary AP has resolved**
:::

## Severe Pancreatitis

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Historical Approach
- Delayed until need for intervention on necrosis declared itself
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Contemporary Data
- >20% of biliary AP patients treated with step-up approach developed biliary complications during wait for cholecystectomy
- **Inflection point: 10 weeks**
- Beyond 10 weeks → increased biliary complications
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Recommendation
Perform cholecystectomy **within 10 weeks** from acute pancreatitis insult — when possible based on clinical disease features
:::


## Overview

Local complications of necrotizing pancreatitis may affect:
- **Alimentary tract**
- **Vascular system** (venous and arterial)
- **Pancreas itself**

## Alimentary Complications

- May arise at any level: stomach, duodenum, small bowel, colon
- **Fistula, stricture, ischemia, obstruction**

::: {.callout-warning}
## Colon Ischemia
- Relatively common (**up to 10%**)
- Usually from **venous thrombosis** with outflow obstruction and congestion
- Consider when patient on steady course **suddenly and rapidly declines**
- Diagnosis very challenging; often requires **laparotomy**
- **New occlusion of SMV/portal vein** may portend colon ischemia
:::

## Venous Thromboembolism (VTE)

::: {.callout-important}
## Remarkably Common in NP
- Incidence **> 50%**
- Large proportion in **splanchnic circulation**
- Extremity DVT also extremely common (**>10-fold higher** than other hospitalized patients)
:::

### Key Findings from Prospective Study

| Finding | Data |
|---------|------|
| Weekly four-extremity screening ultrasound | Validated high incidence of extremity DVT |
| Rapid therapeutic anticoagulation | Prevented PE in all patients without contraindication |
| Anti-factor Xa concentration achieved | Only **21%** of patients |
| No DVT in patients with appropriate anti-factor Xa | Suggests **individualized dosing needed** |

## Visceral Arterial Pseudoaneurysm

::: {.callout-warning}
## Potentially Lethal Complication
- Arises in **4%** of patients with necrotizing pancreatitis
- Location correlates with necrosis distribution
- **Relatively late complication**: diagnosed mean **63 days** into course
:::

### Risk Factors
- Infected necrosis
- Advanced age
- Presence of disconnected pancreatic duct

### Treatment
- **Interventional radiology treatment**
- Almost always definitive

## Pancreatic Complications

### Main Complication: Necrosis Leading to Duct Disruption

| Type | Consequence |
|------|-------------|
| **Isolated duct disruption** | Pancreatic ascites or pancreaticopleural fistula |
| **Major parenchyma necrosis** | Disconnected pancreatic duct syndrome (DPDS) |

### DPDS Management
- Volume of viable upstream pancreas dictates therapeutic decisions
- **Internal drainage** ideal
- **Operative resection** of disconnected tail necessary in many
- Complicated by splenic vein thrombosis with sinistral (left-sided) portal hypertension


## Diagnosis

### When to Suspect
- Clinical condition does not improve or worsens over **first 1-2 weeks**

### Next Step
- Perform **CECT** in search of:
  - Acute necrotic collections
  - Walled-off necrosis

### Proven Infection

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Gas Bubbles on CT
- Caused by gas-forming bacteria
- With or without fistulization to digestive tract
- **Infection considered PROVEN**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### No Gas Bubbles
- Persistent suspicion of infection
- Need for intervention
- Consider **fine-needle aspiration (FNA)**
:::
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## FNA Limitations
- Properly designed prospective studies lacking
- False-negative results in **12-25%** of patients
- Risk of **introducing infection** into necrotic cavity
- **Used infrequently** in current practice
:::

## Treatment Approach

### Antibiotics

- **IV broad-spectrum antibiotics** when infected necrosis suspected or proven
- Tailor based on cultures of infected collection
- **Antibiotics alone** successful in only **5-10%** (small subset)
- In vast majority: antibiotics = **supportive care only**

::: {.callout-important}
## Definitive Treatment
**Drainage and/or necrosectomy** of (suspected) infected necrotic collections
:::

### Timing of Intervention

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Traditional Approach
- Primary laparotomy for necrosectomy
- Used less frequently now
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Contemporary Approach
- Postpone intervention when clinically feasible
- Wait until **walled-off necrosis (full encapsulation)** documented on CECT
- Usually takes **3-4 weeks**
:::
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Why Wait?
Waiting for full encapsulation and delaying intervention **reduces morbidity and mortality** vs. early intervention in first 2 weeks
- Encapsulation facilitates effective necrosectomy
- Reduces risk of bleeding and perforation
:::

### Early Phase Exception

::: {.callout-note}
## Observation Policy
- Sterile collections usually **observed** in acute (early) phase
- Drainage carries risk of **introducing infection**
- Exception: **occasional case of infected necrosis** → prompt early intervention
:::

### Rare Early Drainage Indications
- Obstruction of biliary or GI tract
- Persisting pain
- **Exclusively performed at least 4-6 weeks after onset**


## Emergency Laparotomy Indications

::: {.callout-warning}
## Indicated For
1. **Abdominal compartment syndrome**
2. **Bowel ischemia**
3. **Bowel perforation**

**Goal**: intraabdominal decompression, NOT necrosectomy
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## Critical Recommendation
If early laparotomy needed, **highly recommended NOT to explore retroperitoneum** if infected necrosis has not been documented before operation
:::

### Abdominal Compartment Syndrome
- Extremely rare in clinical practice
- Stepwise approach: medication → percutaneous drainage → laparotomy

## Minimally Invasive Intervention

### Step-Up Approach

::: {.callout-important}
## First Step (Widely Accepted)
Place **percutaneous or endoscopic drain** to decompress collection
:::

### Subsequent Steps

| Step | Action |
|------|--------|
| 1 | Percutaneous/endoscopic drainage |
| 2 | Add or revise drains if no improvement |
| 3 | Necrosectomy if still unsuccessful |

### Advantages of Step-Up Approach
- Reduces surgical trauma vs. primary necrosectomy
- Reduces risk of:
  - Iatrogenic damage
  - Bowel injury
  - Hemorrhage requiring intervention


## Percutaneous Catheter Drainage

### Technique
- Drain placed to relieve pus under pressure
- Prevent further bacteremia
- Serve as **bridge to necrosectomy**

### Advantages
- Simplicity
- Wide availability

### PANTER Trial Results
- **35%** of patients solely treated with antibiotics and percutaneous drains

### Routes

| Route | Advantages |
|-------|-----------|
| **Retroperitoneal** | Preferred; not very demanding, low complication rate (intestinal perforation, contamination) |
| **Transperitoneal** | Alternative when retroperitoneal not feasible |

## Catheter Management

- **Minimum drain size**: 12 French
- **Irrigation**: 3x daily with 250 mL normal saline
- Upsizing or additional drains when collection not optimally drained

::: {.callout-note}
## Current Challenge
Timing of drain upsizing/addition or progression to next "step" is currently **subjective**
:::

## Video-Assisted Retroperitoneal Debridement (VARD)

### When to Proceed
- When drains alone fail to completely evacuate necrosis

### Technique

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Setup
- General anesthesia
- **Right lateral position**
- Subcostal incision: **5-7 cm** near drain entrance
- Use most recent CECT and drain as guidance
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Procedure
1. Find route to peripancreatic collection
2. Remove visible nonadherent necrosis with forceps
3. Using **0-degree videoscope**, remove loosely adherent necrosis with long atraumatic forceps
4. Place two large catheters for postoperative lavage (up to 10L/24h)
:::
:::

## PANTER Trial Evidence

::: {.callout-important}
## Randomized Multicenter Trial
88 patients with suspected infected necrotizing pancreatitis

| Outcome | Step-Up Approach | Primary Open Necrosectomy |
|---------|---------------|--------------------------|
| Mortality + major complications | **40%** | 69% |
| Pancreatic fistula | 28% | 38% |
| Incisional hernia | **7%** | 24% |
| New-onset diabetes | **16%** | 38% |
| Intraabdominal bleeding | 16% | 22% (NS) |
| Enterocutaneous fistula/visceral perforation | 14% | 22% (NS) |

**Step-up approach significantly better!**
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Important Caveat
PANTER trial enrolled highly select patients (88 from 378 screened NP patients)
:::

## Evolution of VARD

Multiple retroperitoneal approaches developed:
- Single-port procedures
- Multiport procedures
- Flexible endoscopy


## Alternative to Surgical Step-Up

**Endoscopic internal transluminal catheter drainage** → followed by **endoscopic transluminal necrosectomy** if drainage incomplete

## Access Routes

- Through **stomach**
- Through **duodenal wall**

## Procedure Steps

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Initial Setup
- Patient in **left lateral position**
- Deep sedation or general anesthesia
- Explore size, content, relationships by **EUS**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### EUS-Guided vs. Non-Guided
- Drainage not guided by ultrasound: technically feasible
- Success rate **inferior** to ultrasound-guided procedure
:::
:::

## Technical Steps

1. Collect material for **bacterial culture**
2. Introduce **19-gauge FNA needle** and guidewire under fluoroscopic guidance → loop in collection
3. Create **8-12 mm fistula tract** using electrocauterization with balloon dilation
4. Place:
   - **Nasocystic catheter**
   - **Two double pigtails** (or metal stents for larger, more permanent opening)

### Post-Procedure
- Used for flushing contents into stomach/duodenum (1L/24h)
- Metal stents may **increase bleeding risk** → remove at short time point (weeks)
- Multiple collections: multiple cystogastrostomies or combined percutaneous + endoscopic drainage

## Endoscopic Necrosectomy

::: {.callout-important}
## When to Perform
If **no clinical improvement within 72 hours** after drainage
:::

### Technique

| Step | Detail |
|------|--------|
| Tract dilation | 15-18 mm with forward viewing endoscope |
| Advancement | Endoscope advanced into collection |
| Instruments | Snares, baskets, nets, forceps |
| Debris | Left in stomach |
| Insufflation | **CO₂ recommended** (reduces air embolism risk, though not 100% protective) |
| Completion | Double pigtail drains left in cavity |

### Follow-Up
- **Repeat every few days** until most necrotic material removed

## Comparative Outcomes

### Single-Institution Series

| Parameter | Endoscopic | Surgical Transgastric |
|-----------|-----------|----------------------|
| Number of procedures | **More** | Fewer |
| Length of stay | **Longer** | Shorter |
| Complications | Higher (likely learning curve) | Lower |

::: {.callout-note}
## Conclusion
Endoscopic and surgical transgastric approaches are **two among many useful approaches**
:::

### Selection Depends On
- Patient factors (physiology, NP etiology, necrosis distribution)
- Local experience
- Local interest


## Current Evidence Status

::: {.callout-warning}
## Key Point
**No convincing evidence** on preferred route of necrosectomy
- Shift toward minimally invasive interventions
- **Superiority of one strategy NOT proven**
:::

## Trial Evidence

### PANTER Trial Limitation
- Did not compare VARD and open necrosectomy directly
- VARD always preceded by percutaneous drainage in step-up approach

### PENGUIN Trial (Pilot, n=20)

| Outcome | Endoscopic | VARD |
|---------|-----------|------|
| Postprocedural proinflammatory response | **Significantly lower** | Higher |

::: {.callout-note}
## Caveat
Clearly **underpowered** for definitive conclusions (18 patients underwent necrosectomy)
:::

### TENSION Trial (n=98)

- Selected from **418 screened patients**
- Endoscopic (n=47) vs. surgical (n=51) step-up approaches

| Primary Endpoint | Result |
|-----------------|--------|
| Major complication or death | **Similar** in both groups |
| Fistula rate | **Lower** in endoscopic group |

## Key Principles

::: {.callout-important}
## Multidisciplinary Team Approach
NP is tremendously **heterogeneous disease process**

**"One size" treatment does NOT fit all patients**

Team should include:
- Surgeons
- Gastroenterologists
- Radiologists
- Intensivists
:::

### Recommendations

1. Most experts recommend some form of **step-up approach**
2. Ideally, **single physician** cares for patient during entire long-term acute illness
3. **Long-term follow-up** extremely important:
   - **>80%** will develop some problem over time
   - Early, midterm, or late follow-up needed


## Key Takeaways

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Epidemiology & Classification
- Most common acute GI hospitalization
- 80% mild, 20% severe
- 2012 Revised Atlanta: mild, moderate, severe
- Interstitial edematous vs. necrotizing
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Diagnosis
- 2 of 3 criteria: pain, enzymes, imaging
- CECT not always required
- Avoid early CECT (72-96h) for necrosis assessment
:::
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Predicting Severity
- Persistent organ failure = key determinant
- Persistent SIRS >48h predicts severity
- Multiple scoring systems available, all with limitations
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Treatment
- Supportive care: pain, fluids, nutrition
- ERCP only for cholangitis
- Early cholecystectomy for mild biliary AP
- Step-up approach for infected necrosis
:::
:::

## Final Message

::: {.callout-important}
## Patient-Centered, Multidisciplinary Care
- Acute pancreatitis is heterogeneous
- Individualize treatment based on patient factors
- Use step-up approach when possible
- Long-term follow-up essential (>80% develop complications)
:::
